Pregnancy

17 to 20 Weeks Pregnant: Movement and the Anatomy Scan

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

At 20 weeks pregnant you are roughly halfway through a 40 week pregnancy, and your baby now measures about 25 cm from crown to heel and weighs around 300 g. The stretch from week 17 to week 20 brings two milestones most parents remember: the first flutters of movement and the anatomy scan. This guide walks through what is developing, how you might feel, and the short list of things worth doing now.

How your baby grows from week 17 to 20

Between weeks 17 and 20, your baby roughly doubles in weight. By week 20, most babies measure about 25 cm from crown to heel, around 10 inches, and weigh close to 300 g, a little over 10 ounces. Part of the jump you see on growth charts is a change in how babies are measured: before 20 weeks, length is usually given from crown to rump, and after that from crown to heel, so the legs suddenly count. Underneath the numbers, steady work is happening. Fat is beginning to form under the skin, muscles are getting stronger, and the movements that once looked random on ultrasound are becoming smoother and more coordinated.

Two protective layers now cover your baby's skin. Vernix is a creamy white coating that shields the skin from the surrounding amniotic fluid, and lanugo is a layer of fine, soft hair that helps hold the vernix in place. Both are normal, and most of each disappears before birth. Hearing is developing quickly in this window too. The inner ear structures are maturing, and many babies begin responding to muffled sounds from your body and, a little later, to voices from outside. Your baby also swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid, which is early practice for feeding, and cycles through sleep and wake periods that may not match yours at all.

How you might feel right now

Somewhere in this stretch, many people feel movement for the first time. Most notice it between 16 and 22 weeks, and it often comes later in a first pregnancy simply because the sensation is easy to miss. Early movement rarely feels like a kick. It is closer to flutters, bubbles, or light tapping that comes and goes, and it is easiest to catch when you are lying down quietly. An anterior placenta, one that sits at the front of the uterus, can cushion the feeling for a few more weeks. If you have felt nothing yet, that is common at this stage and not a sign that something is wrong.

Your body is changing visibly now. The top of the uterus reaches about the level of your belly button around week 20, so the bump is usually hard to hide. Common symptoms in this window include backache as your posture shifts, brief sharp twinges low in the belly when you stand or twist, known as round ligament pain, a stuffy nose, leg cramps at night, and skin changes such as a dark line down the belly or darker patches on the face. Appetite often picks up, and many people have more energy than they did in the first trimester. Comfortable shoes, regular snacks, and side sleeping with a pillow between your knees all start earning their keep.

The anatomy scan, this window's headline appointment

The headline appointment in this window is the anatomy scan, sometimes called the mid-pregnancy ultrasound or the 20 week scan. It is usually done between 18 and 22 weeks. A sonographer takes a long, careful look at how your baby is growing and checks the major organs and structures, from the brain and heart to the spine and limbs, in more detail than earlier scans could. The scan also looks at what surrounds your baby, including where the placenta is attached and how much amniotic fluid is present. It is a screening scan, which means it looks for anything that deserves a closer look. It is not a final verdict on your baby's health.

For many parents this is also the moment they can learn their baby's sex, if the position cooperates and if they want to know. Tell the sonographer at the start if you would rather keep it a surprise. Plan for the appointment to take a while, often 30 to 45 minutes, and follow your clinic's instructions about arriving with a full bladder. Babies do not always pose helpfully, so being asked to walk around, or to return another day for repeat views, is common and usually means nothing more than an awkward angle. Your clinic will talk you through the findings and arrange any follow-up that is needed.

Is 20 weeks really the halfway point?

Twenty weeks is the halfway point in the way pregnancy is usually counted: 40 weeks from the first day of your last period. It is a fair milestone, but hold it loosely. Term is a window rather than a single date, and most babies arrive sometime between 37 and 42 weeks, so your second half may run a little shorter or longer than the first. If your due date was adjusted after an early ultrasound, use your clinic's dating rather than your own calendar math. However you count it, this is a natural moment to look up from week by week symptoms and start thinking about the months ahead.

A short list beats a long one. First, book the anatomy scan if it is not already scheduled, because the 18 to 22 week window passes quickly. Second, start a low-effort movement habit: simply notice when your baby tends to be active, such as after meals or in the evening. There is no need to count anything yet, since formal kick counting belongs to the third trimester. Third, look into childbirth classes now, because popular ones fill up and many run across several weeks. This is also a reasonable time to ask about maternity or parental leave paperwork at work, while there is no urgency behind the question.

Comfort, self-care, and when to call

Small comforts matter more as the bump grows. Side sleeping with a pillow between your knees eases back strain, and rolling to your side before getting up from bed protects the round ligaments. Keep water nearby, keep snacks simple and regular, and use an unscented moisturizer if the skin over your belly feels itchy as it stretches. Gentle exercise such as walking or swimming is encouraged for most people; check with your clinician if you have been told to limit activity. It also helps to keep a running list of questions for the scan appointment. A notebook works well, or you can note dates, symptoms, and questions in the BeMama app so they are ready when you need them.

At this stage, no one expects you to monitor movement formally, and a quiet day is not yet something clinicians ask you to track. Some symptoms should be reported promptly at any stage, though. Call your maternity team right away, rather than waiting for your next appointment, for vaginal bleeding, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, a severe or persistent headache, changes in your vision, a fever, pain or burning when you pass urine, or strong cramping that does not settle with rest. None of these automatically means something is wrong, but each deserves a real conversation rather than a search engine, and your team would much rather hear about a symptom early than have you wait and worry.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pregnancy is dated from the first day of the last menstrual period and is commonly described in weeks and trimesters. ACOG’s week ranges describe typical development, but they are an orientation rather than a test of an individual fetus.

Due dates are estimates, and ultrasound is used for medical reasons to assess gestational age, growth, anatomy, position, and other questions. Only a qualified prenatal professional can interpret findings for a specific pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama’s week view for education, appointment preparation, and dated notes. It cannot confirm fetal growth, anatomy, heartbeat, or wellbeing.

When to seek help

Contact your prenatal team for bleeding, severe pain, fluid leakage, reduced movement after movement is established, or any urgent concern instead of relying on a week-by-week article.

Key takeaways

  • By week 20 your baby measures about 25 cm from crown to heel and weighs around 300 g.
  • First movements are usually felt between 16 and 22 weeks, and often later in a first pregnancy.
  • The anatomy scan happens between 18 and 22 weeks and checks growth, organs, and placenta position.
  • Twenty weeks is roughly halfway through a standard 40 week pregnancy, so it is a good moment to book classes and plan ahead.
  • Report bleeding, leaking fluid, severe headache, vision changes, or fever to your clinician promptly at any stage.

Frequently asked questions

When do you first feel the baby kick?

Most people first feel movement between 16 and 22 weeks of pregnancy. In a first pregnancy it often comes later in that window, because the early flutters are easy to mistake for gas or muscle twitches. An anterior placenta can also cushion the sensation for a few extra weeks. Feeling nothing yet at 17 to 20 weeks is common and usually normal.

What week is the anatomy scan done?

The anatomy scan is usually done between 18 and 22 weeks of pregnancy, most often around week 20. It is a detailed ultrasound that checks your baby's growth and major organs, along with the placenta's position and the amount of amniotic fluid. If yours is not booked yet, contact your clinic soon, because the window is fairly narrow.

Is 20 weeks halfway through pregnancy?

Yes, 20 weeks is roughly the halfway point, because pregnancy is usually counted as 40 weeks from the first day of your last period. In practice the second half varies, since most babies arrive somewhere between 37 and 42 weeks. Treat it as a milestone rather than an exact countdown.

What happens at 18 weeks pregnant?

At 18 weeks your baby is about 14 cm from crown to rump and weighs around 200 g, the ears are settling into position, and hearing is developing. Many people feel the first flutters of movement around this week, though feeling them later is still normal. It is also the earliest week many clinics book the anatomy scan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
